title: Peacekeeping

cards.h: The blue helmets and India's proudest record
cards.b:
UN peacekeeping is the area where India has paid the highest price and earned the most goodwill. Indian soldiers, police and civilians have served in more than 50 missions since 1948. By India's own count (repeated at the UN in November 2026) over 300,000 personnel have served in total, and well over 180 have died.

The topic asks you to know three things: how peacekeeping works and has changed, India's contribution and sacrifices, and India's critique of how mandates are made, which links to its demand for a UNSC seat.

Peacekeeping is not mentioned in the UN Charter. Dag Hammarskjöld called it "Chapter VI and a half".

• Legal basis: the Security Council authorises missions under Chapter VI (peaceful settlement) or, in robust cases, Chapter VII (enforcement). The term 'Chapter six and a half' is attributed to Hammarskjöld.
  • Three classic principles: consent of the parties, impartiality, and non-use of force except in self-defence and defence of the mandate.
  • Early missions: UNTSO (1948, Middle East) and UNMOGIP (1949, India–Pakistan, Kashmir). The first armed force was UNEF I (1956), after Suez, an idea developed by Lester Pearson and Hammarskjöld.
  • Funding: a separate peacekeeping budget with assessed contributions. Troop-contributing countries (TCCs) are reimbursed at a standard rate.

India does not accept that UNMOGIP is relevant after the 1972 Simla Agreement.

After the Cold War, missions began to do more: elections, human rights, police training and state-building. Failures in Somalia (1993), Rwanda (1994) and Srebrenica (1995) led to reform. The Brahimi Report (2000) asked for clear mandates and enough resources. The Responsibility to Protect (R2P) was endorsed at the 2005 World Summit. The Action for Peacekeeping (A4P) initiative came in 2018.

Modern missions face asymmetric threats (Mali, DRC), accusations of sexual exploitation, and a shortage of funds.

Boutros Boutros-Ghali's An Agenda for Peace (1992) separated four ideas. Learn them as a ladder.

Preventive diplomacy

Act before a conflict breaks out: fact-finding, early warning, mediation.

Peacemaking

Bring warring parties to agreement by peaceful means (Chapter VI).

Peacekeeping

Deploy UN personnel, with consent, to hold a ceasefire or help implement a deal.

Peace enforcement

Use force under Chapter VII, even without consent.

Post-conflict peacebuilding

Rebuild institutions and trust. The Peacebuilding Commission was set up in 2005.

India is strong in the third and fifth, and cautious about the fourth.

• Korea (1950s): India led the Custodian Force for prisoners of war and chaired the Neutral Nations Repatriation Commission; a field ambulance unit served in the war.
  • Indochina (1954): chaired the International Control Commissions in Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia.
  • Congo (1960–64): over 6,000 Indian troops. Captain Gurbachan Singh Salaria was awarded the Param Vir Chakra, India's only peacekeeper to receive it.
  • Cyprus (1964–): Lt Gen K.S. Thimayya, Force Commander of UNFICYP, died in service in December 1965.
  • Other: Gaza (UNEF), Somalia, Rwanda, Angola, Sierra Leone (UNAMSIL), Namibia (UNTAG, Lt Gen Prem Chand as Force Commander), the former Yugoslavia (UNPROFOR, Lt Gen Satish Nambiar as first Force Commander), Lebanon (UNIFIL), Golan (UNDOF), South Sudan (UNMISS), DR Congo (MONUSCO), Abyei (UNISFA).

• All-women unit: in 2007 India sent the first all-female formed police unit to Liberia (UNMIL), a major source of inspiration. It served until 2016.
  • Sacrifice: India says over 180 of its peacekeepers have died, the highest toll of any country (the count changes a little each year).
  • Today: India is among the larger contributors of troops in recent years, with a few thousand personnel in UN missions, mainly in South Sudan, Lebanon, DRC, Golan and Abyei. In 2026 about 600 are in UNIFIL, Lebanon. India has said it is the largest cumulative contributor.
  • Training: the Centre for UN Peacekeeping (CUNPK) in New Delhi, set up in 2000, trains Indian and foreign peacekeepers.
  • Leadership: Indian generals have commanded forces in UNTAG, UNPROFOR and MONUSCO.

• Say in mandates: TCCs do the dying but have little voice in drafting mandates. India pushes consultations (Resolution 1353, 2001, created consultation meetings).
  • Safety: India led the push for Resolution 2589 (August 2021), adopted during its UNSC presidency, on accountability for crimes against peacekeepers.
  • Technology and training: India backs digital tools for peacekeepers and offers medical help and training.
  • Rules of engagement: India is cautious about robust enforcement and about missions that become parties to conflict.
  • Consent and sovereignty: India insists on host-state consent and a UN mandate for any deployment. It did not send troops to Iraq (2003) without a UN mandate.

The deeper argument: those who contribute most should have a seat at the table.

cards.h: Do the benefits justify the cost?
cards.b:
Realists say contribution gives little real power: the P5 still decide. Liberals see value in shared norms and leadership in global order. India's argument: peacekeeping is both a moral duty and a case for reform. The UN's financial difficulties and US funding cuts in 2025–26 also threaten missions and reimbursements.

Another view, from scholars of peacekeeping: India's choice of safe mission areas with a stable consent environment follows its tradition of respect for state sovereignty.

• India stresses women, peace and security: more women peacekeepers and a gender-balanced role.
  • It supports technology (digital tools, drones), medical care and training through CUNPK.
  • In November 2026 it called at the UN for better-resourced and better-protected missions.
  • It links peacekeeping to UNSC reform: "those who sacrifice should decide".
  • Peacekeepers also serve under pressure in Lebanon amid the broader West Asia conflict.

"Evaluate India's contribution to UN peacekeeping. How does it relate to India's claim for a permanent UNSC seat?" (typical)
"Discuss the challenges facing UN peacekeeping in the 21st century." (typical)
"Explain the principles of UN peacekeeping and the Brahimi Report." (typical)

Structure: (1) concept and legal basis; (2) principles; (3) evolution and failures; (4) India's contribution: missions, firsts, sacrifices; (5) India's critique and conditions; (6) link to UN reform; (7) way forward.

quiz.q: Peacekeeping is sometimes described as 'Chapter six and a half' because it:
o: Lies between peaceful settlement and enforcement
quiz.w: It is not mentioned in the Charter and sits between Chapters VI and VII.

quiz.q: The first UN mission to India–Pakistan was:
quiz.w: UNMOGIP (1949) monitors the ceasefire line in Kashmir.

quiz.q: India's only peacekeeper to receive the Param Vir Chakra was:
India sent the first all-women formed police unit to:
quiz.w: In 2007, to the UN Mission in Liberia.

quiz.q: The Brahimi Report on UN peace operations was published in:
quiz.w: The Report of the Panel on UN Peace Operations (2000).

quiz.q: Who was the first Force Commander of UNPROFOR in the former Yugoslavia?
quiz.w: Lt Gen Satish Nambiar of India (1992).

quiz.q: UNSC Resolution 2589 (2021), adopted during India's presidency, concerns:
quiz.w: It was adopted unanimously on 18 August 2021.

quiz.q: Which report of 2015 reviewed UN peace operations?
quiz.w: The High-level Independent Panel on Peace Operations.

quiz.q: The Centre for UN Peacekeeping (CUNPK) is located in:
quiz.w: New Delhi, set up in 2000 by the United Service Institution of India.

quiz.q: India's insistence for sending troops abroad is that deployment must have:
o: A UN mandate and host consent
quiz.w: India generally deploys only under a UN mandate with host-state consent.
